item.title: Finance Ministry clarifies $18.5m digital wallet balance
item.description: The Ministry of Finance has clarified that the $18.5 million held in M-PAiSA and MyCash accounts at the end of July 2022 was retained to support future Government digital payments, with the balance now reduced to about $3.18 million. Permanent Secretary for Finance Shiri Gounder said the funds had subsequently been used for programs including inflation mitigation payments, bus fare subsidies and b
item.content:encoded:
The Ministry of Finance has clarified that the $18.5 million held in M-PAiSA and MyCash accounts at the end of July 2022 was retained to support future Government digital payments, with the balance now reduced to about $3.18 million.

Permanent Secretary for Finance Shiri Gounder said the funds had subsequently been used for programs including inflation mitigation payments, bus fare subsidies and back-to-school assistance.

The clarification follows concerns highlighted in the Compliance Audit Report over the $18.5 million remaining with the two service providers after the completion of a Government assistance program.

Mr Gounder said M-PAiSA and MyCash had become important components of Government’s payment infrastructure, with almost $500 million disbursed through the platforms since 2020.

“Given that M-PAiSA and MyCash have become a key feature of our payment platform, we need to ensure that sufficient cash balances are maintained in these digital wallets to meet our payment needs,” he said.

“This is same as how Government maintains funds at the commercial banks for its daily operations.”

Mr Gounder said the digital wallets effectively served a similar purpose to bank accounts used for Government payments.

“Since the end of July 2022, Government has used the M-PAiSA and MyCash funds for payment of inflation mitigation payout, bus fare subsidy and back to school support,” he said.

“The current balance as of July 2026 stands at around $3.18 million.”

The Standing Committee on Public Accounts had noted in its review of the Compliance Audit Report that $18,511,428 remained with the service providers following the completion of the program.

The audit said the Ministry had advised that the Permanent Secretary approved retaining the funds for future initiatives, but auditors could not sight documentary evidence authorising the retention.

Mr Gounder, however, said proper controls and records were maintained in accordance with Government’s financial rules and regulations.

“Records are well maintained and easily available for reconciliation and audit verification and a standard operating procedure exists as to how digital wallet funds will be utilised and captured in the Government accounts,” he said.

He also said the Ministry had raised the matter with the Office of the Auditor-General during the audit process.

“The Ministry had clarified the above with the Office of the Auditor-General during the audit exit meeting, however, it seems that this was not explained appropriately in the audit report,” Mr Gounder said.

item.title: Two more arrested over viral Nadi taxi robbery
item.description: Two more suspects have been taken into Police custody in connection with the aggravated robbery of a taxi driver in Nadi that was captured on a dash camera and went viral on social media. Their arrests bring the number of suspects in custody to three, while the Western Division Taskforce continues to search for a fourth suspect whose identity is known to Police.
item.content:encoded:
Two more suspects have been taken into Police custody in connection with the aggravated robbery of a taxi driver in Nadi that was captured on a dash camera and went viral on social media.

Their arrests bring the number of suspects in custody to three, while the Western Division Taskforce continues to search for a fourth suspect whose identity is known to Police.

The incident occurred at around 8am yesterday and was captured by the taxi’s dash camera.

Footage of the incident, which subsequently went viral, showed the taxi driver pleading for his life during the alleged attack.

A 23-year-old man became the first suspect to be taken into custody after handing himself over to Police yesterday evening.

He was taken to the Lautoka Police Station for questioning.

Investigations into the alleged aggravated robbery continue.

item.title: PM more focused on personal legacy – Seruiratu
item.description: Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu has accused Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka of being more focused on securing his personal legacy than addressing the immediate concerns of Fijians, as debate continues over constitutional and electoral reforms ahead of the next General Election. Mr Seruiratu said Fiji was only months away from the dissolution of Parliament and questioned whether there was sufficien
item.content:encoded:
Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu has accused Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka of being more focused on securing his personal legacy than addressing the immediate concerns of Fijians, as debate continues over constitutional and electoral reforms ahead of the next General Election.

Mr Seruiratu said Fiji was only months away from the dissolution of Parliament and questioned whether there was sufficient time to undertake major constitutional amendments, electoral reforms, public consultations and any potential referendum before the election.

“It is disappointing that the Prime Minister appears more focused on securing his personal legacy than on putting the people of Fiji first,” Mr Seruiratu said.

He said the Coalition Government had almost four years to pursue constitutional and electoral reforms and should have acted earlier if they were a genuine priority.

“The Prime Minister is wishfully thinking if he believes these processes can be undertaken in a credible, transparent and democratic manner within the limited time that remains,” he said.

Mr Seruiratu said the Government’s priority should instead be the everyday pressures confronting Fijians.

“At a time when Fijians are struggling with the rising cost of living, concerns over healthcare, crime, infrastructure and economic uncertainty, the Prime Minister should be focused on addressing the issues affecting everyday families,” he said.

Mr Seruiratu also warned against any move that could delay the General Election, saying changing the timetable at this stage could create political and constitutional uncertainty.

“More importantly, any attempt to delay the General Election risks creating a constitutional crisis,” he said.

“Altering the timetable at this late stage would undermine public confidence and create unnecessary political and constitutional uncertainty.”

He also expressed concern that the constitutional review process was being rushed and said ordinary Fijians needed a meaningful opportunity to participate.

“The Constitution belongs to the people of Fiji,” Mr Seruiratu said.

“Any changes must be undertaken carefully and with genuine public participation — not rushed through to satisfy political timelines.”

Mr Seruiratu said the Electoral Commission had indicated it was ready to conduct the next General Election and called on Government to respect the constitutional timetable.

“The Government should respect that timetable and allow the people of Fiji to exercise their democratic right to choose their next government,” he said.

item.title: Dolly Parton, queen of country music, dies at 80
item.description: Dolly Parton was around six when she wrote her first song: “Little Tiny Tasseltop,” an ode to her corncob doll with corn-silk hair. item.content:encoded:
Dolly Parton was around six when she wrote her first song: “Little Tiny Tasseltop,” an ode to her corncob doll with corn-silk hair. Her mother stored it preciously in a shoebox.

“I loved that little doll,” Parton wrote decades later. “I expressed myself and my feelings through writing – I’m sure what I was thinking was, ‘Well, Tasseltop has to have a song about her.’”

Parton never stopped making music after that. The irrepressible country music singer, songwriter and actress whose charisma, heartfelt lyrics and business acumen captured the public’s imagination for nearly six decades, died on Tuesday aged 80, her family said in a statement.

She won 11 Grammy awards, including a Lifetime Achievement Award.

With classic songs including “Coat of Many Colors,” “Jolene” and “I Will Always Love You,” she became one of the best-selling female artists of all time, with over 100 million records sold.

Parton’s wholesome personality, combined with her towering blond hairdos, flamboyant costumes and giddy delight at holding center stage, endeared her to Americans of all backgrounds and helped introduce country music to international audiences.

Over the years Parton hosted a TV variety show, starred in movies, and even created a theme park, Dollywood, a popular tourist spot in her home state of Tennessee – all in addition to her lauded work as a songwriter.

But the quality that gave her enduring star power was her ability to connect with people. Coming from a self-described “dirt-poor” family, Parton often stood in as a symbol of the working-class American and regularly threw her name and money behind causes she believed in.

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, Parton donated $1 million to vaccine research at Vanderbilt University in 2020, making her an early sponsor of Moderna’s vaccine development.

She conducted a literacy program for preschool children across the United States, as well as in Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and Ireland, and provided scholarships to high school students in the Tennessee county where she was born.

The county erected a life-size statue of her in front of the courthouse in thanks, though she declined another proposed statue of her in Nashville in 2021, saying, “Given all that’s going on in the world, I don’t think putting me on a pedestal is appropriate at this time.”

It was this ability to stay true to her roots, combined with her drive to work hard and her nonpartisanship, that fueled her appeal among conservatives and liberals in a politically polarized America.

Dolly Rebecca Parton was born on January 19, 1946, in Pittman Center, Tennessee, and grew up in a one-room cabin in nearby Locust Ridge. One of 12 children of tobacco farmer Robert Lee Parton, her difficult childhood gave credibility to her often personal songs trilled in a distinctive soprano.

Her mother, Avie Lee, would sing constantly – songs from England, Ireland and Wales that told a story. “Mama had this haunting voice, and Lord you would feel it,” Parton wrote in her 2020 book “Dolly Parton, Songteller” co-authored with Robert K. Oermann.

Parton got her first real guitar when she was eight. Her mother would say, whenever she had guests: “I want you to hear this song this little thing has made up. It’s really good.” Parton loved the attention.

She was singing on a local radio station by age 11, and at age 13 was appearing on the Grand Ole Opry, a weekly country music concert in Nashville, Tennessee.

After graduating from high school, she moved to Nashville to pursue a music career and began a famous partnership with country music singer Porter Wagoner, which would include a years-long stint on his TV show and 14 top-ten duets. She penned her hit song “I Will Always Love You” as a farewell to Wagoner when she decided to pursue a solo career.

On the first day Parton arrived in country music’s capital, she met Carl Dean, an asphalt paver. They would marry two years later, in 1966. Throughout their long marriage, Dean shunned the spotlight and did not tour with her, though he would be a muse for many of her greatest hits, including “Jolene,” which was inspired by a red-haired bank teller’s crush on Dean.

Her own appearance was the object of intense interest. Initially embarrassed, she eventually found the humor in frequent questions about her extravagant dress sense and generous figure.

She dismissed rumors that her breasts were insured and laughed off periodic rumors that she was bedridden due to their weight, telling People magazine: “Well, they are heavy, but they haven’t crippled me yet.”

Parton patterned her signature look on a woman she would see walking around her Tennessee hometown in tight skirts and high heels, with red nails, red lipstick and peroxided hair. “I thought she was beautiful. But everybody said, ‘She’s trash!’ Parton wrote in her 2023 book “Behind the Seams: My Life in Rhinestones.” “I laughed and said, ‘Well, if that’s trash, that’s what I want to be when I grow up!’”

But as much as she embraced her signature look, she also viewed it as distinct from herself. “I look one way and am another,” she told Ladies’ Home Journal in 1982. “It makes for a good combination. I always think of ‘her,’ the Dolly image, like a ventriloquist does his dummy. I have fun with it. I think, what will I do with her this year to surprise people? What’ll she wear? What’ll she say?”

She also expressed the wish that her appearance would serve to sell, rather than overshadow, her talent.

Her music gained a following not only among the public but also with fellow singers who widely covered her songs – perhaps most famously Whitney Houston’s rendition of “I Will Always Love You.” Some of Parton’s most beloved covers and duets were with her goddaughter, American pop star Miley Cyrus, and Cyrus’ father, country music star Billy Ray Cyrus.

“Jolene” was covered by artists as varied as Beyoncé and The White Stripes.

While Parton was a force on stage and an accomplished vocalist, what set her apart from her peers was her talent with words. Parton wrote every one of her hit songs. All told, she penned an estimated 3,000 throughout her life, though she recorded only about 450 of them.

“I love to write poetic songs and sing flowery words,” she wrote in “Dolly Parton, Songteller.” “I like to make you see something visually, so I want to paint a picture. And I love to come up with clever lines, not just like a songwriter, but like a poet.”

Parton made her movie debut in 1980’s “9 to 5,” starring alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin, with the title tune earning Parton an Oscar nomination for songwriting. She got another Oscar songwriting nomination in 2006 for “Travelin’ Thru,” written for the film “Transamerica.”

Her other movie acting roles included “The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas,” “Steel Magnolias,” “Rhinestone” and “Straight Talk.”

Twenty-five of her songs reached No. 1 on the Billboard Country charts and she was a member of the Songwriters Hall of Fame, receiving its highest honor, the Johnny Mercer Award, in 2007. She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.

item.title: Nath calls for action as taxi drivers face robberies
item.description: Opposition MP Vijay Nath has called for stronger measures to protect taxi drivers following reports of robberies and assaults in Nadi, Wainibokasi and other parts of the country. Mr Nath said the incidents should not be treated as isolated cases, warning they highlighted wider concerns about the safety of people providing an essential public service.
item.content:encoded:
Opposition MP Vijay Nath has called for stronger measures to protect taxi drivers following reports of robberies and assaults in Nadi, Wainibokasi and other parts of the country.

Mr Nath said the incidents should not be treated as isolated cases, warning they highlighted wider concerns about the safety of people providing an essential public service.

“A taxi driver should not have to wonder whether the next passenger entering his or her vehicle poses a threat,” Mr Nath said.

“These drivers are simply trying to earn an honest living, and they deserve to be able to return home safely to their families at the end of their shift.”

He called on the Government, Fiji Police Force and other relevant authorities to take practical steps to improve driver safety, including increased police visibility and patrols in areas where drivers were particularly vulnerable at night.

Mr Nath also called for a faster and more effective system for drivers to seek police assistance during emergencies.

He said authorities should consider measures including CCTV cameras, GPS tracking and other affordable in-vehicle safety technology.

Police, the Land Transport Authority, taxi associations and drivers should also work together to identify high-risk locations and develop appropriate safety measures, he said.

Mr Nath said people who deliberately targeted taxi drivers for robbery or assault should “face the full force of the law”.

He also called for stronger enforcement against illegal taxi operators while ensuring the concerns of licensed drivers were addressed.

However, Mr Nath said safety responsibilities also extended to taxi drivers, who were expected to provide professional and safe services and comply with laws governing the industry.

“Safety must work both ways — passengers should feel safe when entering a taxi, and drivers should feel safe when accepting a passenger,” he said.

“No person should have to choose between earning an honest living and risking their life.”

Mr Nath urged authorities to act before another driver or member of the public became a victim.

“Our taxi drivers are fathers, mothers, husbands, wives and members of our communities trying to make an honest living,” he said.

“They deserve to work in safety and to be treated with dignity and respect.”

item.title: Committee questions $18.5m retained funds with M-Paisa and MyCash
item.description: The Standing Committee on Public Accounts has raised concerns over more than $18.5 million in unused funds that remained with M-Paisa and MyCash after the completion of a government program, with auditors unable to sight documentary evidence authorising the retention. In its review report on the Compliance Audit Report, the committee noted that $18,511,428 remained with the two service providers f
item.content:encoded:
The Standing Committee on Public Accounts has raised concerns over more than $18.5 million in unused funds that remained with M-Paisa and MyCash after the completion of a government program, with auditors unable to sight documentary evidence authorising the retention.

In its review report on the Compliance Audit Report, the committee noted that $18,511,428 remained with the two service providers following the completion of the programs, namely the COVID-19 Cash Assistance Program and the Food Ration Distribution Program.

The Ministry of Finance informed auditors that the Permanent Secretary had approved retaining the money for future initiatives.

However, the audit found that documentary evidence supporting that approval could not be sighted.

The committee said the situation raised concerns about transparency and compliance with financial management requirements.

It recommended that formal documentary approval be maintained whenever government funds are retained in service provider accounts after the completion of a program.

“Ensure unutilized balances are either promptly returned to the Consolidated Fund or formally reallocated with clear authorization,” the committee recommended.

The committee also stressed the need for stronger procedures governing the management of public funds, particularly during emergency or unpredictable situations.

“The Committee further emphasizes the importance of developing clear guidelines, procedures, and protocols to address future unpredictable events,” the report stated.

It said structured frameworks should be established covering risk assessments, documentation requirements and digital verification.

“Establishing structured frameworks for risk assessment, documentation standards, and digital verification mechanisms will ensure that emergency responses are not only swift but also transparent, accountable, and resilient,” the committee said.

The findings highlight the committee’s push for a clear audit trail when unused government funds remain outside the Consolidated Fund following the completion of publicly funded programs.

item.title: Millions paid to insurance company, but few benefited – Kiran
item.description: Government decided to end its welfare insurance scheme after determining that only $33.8 million of about $60 million spent on the program reached beneficiaries through direct insurance payouts, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week. Speaking on the cessation of the welfare insurance scheme, Ms Kiran said the figures showed the insurance model was
item.content:encoded:
Government decided to end its welfare insurance scheme after determining that only $33.8 million of about $60 million spent on the program reached beneficiaries through direct insurance payouts, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week.

Speaking on the cessation of the welfare insurance scheme, Ms Kiran said the figures showed the insurance model was an inefficient way of delivering assistance to vulnerable Fijians.

“Out of that $60 million, only $33.8 million actually reached our citizens as direct payouts,” she said.

Ms Kiran said in the 2023-2024 financial year, Government paid $7.1 million in insurance premiums while claims totalled $3.8 million.

In 2024-2025, premiums increased to $7.2 million, but claims again amounted to $3.8 million.

For the 2025-2026 financial year, she said $7.7 million was paid in premiums while only $3 million was paid out in claims.

“On average, a mere 56 percent of the total funds paid out by the government ended up in the hands of the beneficiaries,” Ms Kiran said.

“The remaining 44 percent did not serve our poor. Instead, it was absorbed by administrative friction, overheads and private corporate margins.”

She told Parliament no responsible government could regard the loss of 44 per cent of welfare funding through the delivery mechanism as economically sustainable.

“In macroeconomics, we call this a deadweight loss to our public finances,” she said.

Ms Kiran said Government had been spending about $7 million annually to provide insurance coverage for approximately 100,000 welfare recipients.

However, she said the insurance framework had processed an average of only about 5,000 claims annually over the past five years.

“We are paying massive premium blocks for a system where 95 percent of the covered population see no tangible touchpoint or benefit in any given year,” she said.

Ms Kiran said the figures demonstrated why Government could no longer justify continuing with the existing welfare insurance arrangement.

item.title: PAC audit report flags 12,602 duplicate COVID Payments
item.description: More than 12,000 duplicate payments worth $630,100 were made during the second round of Fiji’s COVID-19 Cash Assistance Program, according to findings highlighted in the Compliance Audit Report. The Standing Committee on Public Accounts, in reviewing the report, noted that auditors identified 12,602 duplicate payments in Round 2 of the assistance program.
item.content:encoded:
More than 12,000 duplicate payments worth $630,100 were made during the second round of Fiji’s COVID-19 Cash Assistance Program, according to findings highlighted in the Compliance Audit Report.

The Standing Committee on Public Accounts, in reviewing the report, noted that auditors identified 12,602 duplicate payments in Round 2 of the assistance program.

While recovery processes were subsequently introduced in Round 3, the report found that 62 duplicate payments worth $3,100 remained unrecovered, pointing to continuing weaknesses in payment controls.

The committee has called for stronger system controls to prevent duplicate applications and payments.

It also recommended authorities “ensure full recovery of overpayments and maintain transparent reporting of recovery actions.”

Concerns were also raised about reconciliation processes for cash disbursements.

According to the report, reconciliations did not contain documented sign-offs from those preparing and reviewing them.

This meant auditors could not confirm that the reconciliations had been independently prepared and reviewed within the required timeframe.

The committee recommended that documented sign-offs by preparers and reviewers be mandatory for all reconciliations to demonstrate independent preparation and timely review.

The findings relate to the COVID-19 Cash Assistance Program, which was delivered over five rounds and distributed more than $226 million in assistance.

Round 1 provided $90 each to 118,000 applicants, while recipients in Rounds 2 and 3 received $50 each.

Payments increased substantially in the final two rounds, with eligible recipients receiving $360 each.

Round 4 covered 294,924 recipients and distributed about $105.7 million, while Round 5 provided assistance to 241,347 applicants, with approximately $87.5 million distributed.

Overall, more than one million applicant payments were recorded across the five rounds as Government progressively expanded financial support during the COVID-19 period.
